summary: This RFC discusses how to treat several local networks at a site as one Internet network, hiding the internal connections from the outside. It looks at how to do address resolution for this arrangement and proposes approaches.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 925 proposes a way for several local networks to share one Internet network number. Special computers answer address requests and forward data between the local networks, while ordinary hosts continue to use ARP.

questions: how to treat multiple lans as one ip network
what is multi lan address resolution
how does an arp based bridge work
subtitle: A proposal for hiding several connected LANs behind one Internet network address.

tldr.problem: A site with several LANs may want them to appear as one Internet network without exposing their internal connections to outside hosts and gateways.
tldr.mechanism: An ARP-based bridge, called a BOX in the RFC, keeps address caches for its LANs and answers or relays ARP requests for hosts on other LANs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 925 proposes transparent subnets and asks the Internet community for discussion and improvements. The batch metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

facts.label: Suggested timer values
facts.value: T1 under one minute; T2 ten minutes; T3 one hour

today: The batch metadata gives RFC 925 no recorded status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text presents a proposed protocol and requests discussion and suggestions for improvement.

sections.title: The Multi-LAN Problem
sections.content:
The memo considers how a site can treat several local area networks as one Internet network. It argues that the connections between those LANs should be hidden from outside hosts and gateways.

As background, ARP lets a host ask for the hardware address associated with an Internet address. Hosts on the LAN receive the request, and the host with that address can answer.
sections.plainLanguage: A site may connect several LANs but want them to appear as one network from the outside. RFC 925 proposes handling this inside the site, without requiring ordinary hosts to learn the layout.

sections.title: The ARP-Based Bridge
sections.content:
The proposal adds a computer called a BOX, attached to two or more LANs. It keeps recent Internet-address-to-hardware-address mappings for each interface and learns the sender's mapping from each ARP request it receives.

If a mapping is known on the LAN where a request arrived, the BOX stays silent. If the mapping is known on another LAN, it replies with its own hardware address and forwards later datagrams to the destination host.
sections.plainLanguage: The BOX remembers which hardware addresses it has seen on each LAN. It answers for a host on another LAN and then forwards that host's incoming datagrams.

sections.title: Finding Unknown Hosts and Avoiding Loops
sections.content:
When the BOX has no mapping, it records the search and sends ARP requests through its other interfaces. A reply updates the relevant cache and lets the BOX answer the original request. If there is no reply, the search entry remains until it times out because ARP has no negative response.

Search entries stop the same unknown-host request from being relayed indefinitely. The RFC defines timers T1, T2 and T3 with T1 less than T2 and T2 less than T3, and suggests less than one minute, ten minutes and one hour respectively. BOXes also decrement the IP Time-To-Live and update the header checksum when forwarding datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: The BOX records each search before asking other LANs, so it does not relay the same request in a loop. Search and address records expire, and forwarded datagrams have their IP Time-To-Live reduced to limit loops.

sections.title: Transparent and Explicit Subnets
sections.content:
RFC 925 argues for transparent subnets, where hosts use ARP and need not know which LAN contains a destination. It contrasts this with explicit subnets, where addresses include a subnet field and hosts must distinguish local from remote LANs.

The proposal says transparent subnets can let a host move between LANs without changing its Internet address and do not require BOXes to exchange topology information. It also notes that very complex or unbalanced networks may be better served by a BOX-to-BOX routing protocol. The memo asks the Internet community to agree on a solution.
sections.plainLanguage: With this proposal, hosts use the same address-resolution process whether a destination is nearby or on another LAN. The author notes that complex layouts may need a separate routing method between BOXes.

references.text: Plummer, D., "An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol or Converting Network Protocol Addresses to 48-bit Ethernet Addresses for Transmission on Ethernet Hardware", RFC 826, November 1982.
